pedagogy.problem_statement: Most homemade masala chai tastes either flat and watery or harshly bitter and astringent because spices and tea leaves are steeped simultaneously in cold milk rather than extracted through sequential thermodynamic decoction and casein protein binding.
pedagogy.core_thesis: Authentic masala chai is culinary chemistry operating across two thermodynamic phases: polar water decoction at 100°C maximizes spice volatile oil release and polyphenol mass transfer without lipid barrier interference, followed by milk protein emulsification where casein micelles encapsulate astringent tannins into a velvety, aromatic emulsion.
pedagogy.mental_model: A two-stage molecular lock: Stage 1 dissolves volatile aromatic oils and rich tea pigment into polar water; Stage 2 introduces milk proteins that encapsulate sharp tannins like a flavor shield while lipids dissolve non-polar spice essences.
pedagogy.key_takeaway: Always crack spices coarsely and decoct in water first; milk added too early coats tea leaves in fat and blocks extraction, while whole milk added post-decoction binds harsh catechins into a smooth emulsion.
verified_claims: Coarsely crushing cardamom, cloves, cinnamon, and ginger fractures plant cell walls to release volatile oils (cineole, eugenol, cinnamaldehyde, gingerol) without grinding cellular debris into bitter cloudiness.
Water at 100°C acts as a high-polarity solvent extracting water-soluble polyphenols and flavonoids with 4x faster mass transfer than fatty milk suspensions.
Milk casein proteins form hydrophobic and hydrogen-bonded complexes with tea tannins (theaflavins and thearubigins), neutralizing oral astringency without diminishing aromatic perception.
The rolling double-boil creates convective turbulence that homogenizes milk lipids into fine droplets, producing microfoam and rich caramelization when poured from height.
anti_patterns: Do not boil tea leaves and spices in cold milk from the start; milk lipids coat the leaf cuticle and suppress extraction by up to 60%.
Do not use pre-ground powdered spices; exposed essential oils oxidize rapidly and leave sediment that tastes muddy and astringent.
Do not steep at low temperatures (below 90°C); spice decoction requires boiling convection to dissolve hydrophobic oil droplets into the brew.

scene_blueprint.title: The Spices & The Coarse Crush
scene_blueprint.pedagogical_objective: Demonstrate that coarse cracking releases volatile essential oils without releasing bitter tannin dust.
scene_blueprint.visual_action: Botanical cards fracture under mortar impact, releasing expanding glowing volatile oil particles.

scene_blueprint.title: Water First: The Decoction Phase
scene_blueprint.pedagogical_objective: Explain why boiling in water first achieves 85% extraction efficiency without milk fats blocking the tea leaf cuticle.
scene_blueprint.visual_action: Convective decoction flask drawing golden Catmull-Rom diffusion waves into boiling water at 100°C.

scene_blueprint.title: The Milk & Casein Shield
scene_blueprint.pedagogical_objective: Show how casein micelles bind bitter tannins to neutralize astringency while milk lipids dissolve spice aromatics.
scene_blueprint.visual_action: Milk cream swirls into deep tea amber, casein micelles encapsulating sharp tannin molecules into smooth emulsion.

scene_blueprint.title: The Double Boil & The Perfect Pour
